title: Trace a Word on a Letter Grid
statement:
You get a grid board of lowercase letters and a string word. Decide whether you can spell word by starting at some cell and stepping each time to a cell that shares a side with the current one: up, down, left or right, never diagonally.

Each cell can be used at most once in the word. Return true if the word can be traced and false otherwise.

examples.why: m → a → t → s: right, down, right.
The only t next to the a is the one you started on. Stepping back onto it would use a cell twice.
From g there are two o's. The one below dead-ends, so the search must back up and go right instead.

constraints: board and word hold lowercase English letters
hints: Try every cell as the start. From a cell holding word[k], where can word[k + 1] be?
Recurse into each of the four neighbours that holds the next letter. The danger is walking back onto a cell this path already uses. How do you remember which cells those are?
Mark the current cell as used (for example overwrite it with '#'), search the four neighbours for the rest of the word, then restore the letter before returning. Stop as soon as any branch succeeds.

explain.intuition:
The same template, on a grid. A node is a path of cells that spells the first k letters. Its children are the up-to-four neighbours that hold letter k + 1 and are not on the path yet. The answer is true as soon as any path reaches length word.length, so this search returns early instead of collecting everything.

The state to choose and un-choose here is which cells are on the current path. The cheap way to track it is to overwrite the cell with # while you are on it, so no neighbour check can match it, and to write the letter back when you leave. That restore is the un-choose step. Without it, a dead-end branch would leave its cells blocked, and a later branch could not use them: on [["t", "o"], ["o", "o"]], a first try for "oot" that starts at the top o and dead-ends would block the cells the real answer needs. Without the mark at all, a path can step back onto itself, as in "tat".
steps: For every cell, start dfs(r, c, 0). Return true if any start succeeds.
In dfs(r, c, k): return false if the cell is outside the grid or does not hold word[k]. Return true if k is the last index.
Choose: save the letter and overwrite the cell with #.
Explore: found = dfs(r+1, c, k+1) || dfs(r-1, c, k+1) || dfs(r, c+1, k+1) || dfs(r, c-1, k+1).
Un-choose: write the letter back, then return found.
pitfalls: Not marking the cell. "tat" then walks t → a → the same t and returns true.
Returning true from inside the loop before restoring the cell. That leaves a # on the board, which breaks later searches if the board is reused.
Looking at diagonal neighbours. "mt" on the first board is not a valid trace.

complexity.time: O(R · C · 3^L), L = word length: after the first step, each cell has at most 3 unused neighbours

solutions.title: Backtracking from every cell
solutions.idea: Start from each cell. Step into neighbours that hold the next letter, marking the cell as used while it is on the path and restoring it afterwards.

solutions.title: Backtracking with letter-count pruning
solutions.idea: Before searching, check that the board has enough of every letter the word needs. Then start from the rarer end: if the last letter is rarer than the first, search for the reversed word.
solutions.time: O(R · C · 3^L) worst case, far less in practice

followups: Many words must be checked against the same board. How do you avoid searching the board once per word?
Steps may now also go diagonally. What changes in the code and in the bound?
